1:
The call to return is measured by how far it must go. Gill insists on a thorough return, not halfway but quite up to the seat, falling down and acknowledging sin while taking hold of God by faith; and he grounds the appeal on the fact that he is still their God, by choice, by covenant, by redemption and by their own profession, and is ready to receive them. Ellicott finds the same tenderness in a single pronoun, and quotes the rabbinic saying that repentance presses right up to the eternal throne. Henry works both halves of the verse into a pair of lessons: sin is a fall, and those who have fallen by it must get up again by repentance; and conversion must be preached to those inside the church as well as to the heathen, since being Israel makes the revolt more heinous and the return more necessary.

Calvin has to answer an objection before he can accept the invitation at all. He had said earlier that no remedy remained, because the people had provoked God past bearing, and he now seems to contradict himself. His solution is a distinction he thinks carefully worth noticing: the earlier threat of final destruction had the whole body of the people in view, while this address turns to the few who had remained faithful. Without that distinction, he says, a reader will find himself perplexed in many parts of scripture.

Clarke reads the chapter as a designed sequence and lays it out. The vengeance denounced at the end of the previous chapter leads the prophet to exhort repentance, and he furnishes a form of prayer suitable to the occasion; God then makes large promises, using the copious dews that refresh green herbs as a figure for the refreshing comforts of the gospel; the reformation from idolatry and the prosperity that follows come next under the emblem of a flourishing tree; and the whole is confined at the last to those who bring forth the fruits of righteousness. He also holds that the evils, positively predicted as they are, might yet have been prevented.

Taking words is treated as more than a form of speech. Gill will not have mere words without the heart, but words that express its true sense, words of confession by which sin is acknowledged and forgiveness asked. Clarke turns it into a doctrine of prayer: a man may be assured he prays rightly when he uses the words God himself has put in his mouth, which is what gives the Lord's Prayer a potency beyond any human composition, and probably why the reformers set it so often in the public liturgy. He then numbers the steps the verse prescribes, from believing the invitations true and casting aside the idols to pleading the very words by which one was encouraged, deploring the iniquity, and letting faith receive what God waits to impart.

The last clause is a crux, and the readers differ over what is being offered. Ellicott renders it accept of good, and we will render as calves our lips, so that the words of true repentance become the offering in place of animals, and he points to other places where words are put into penitents' lips in the same way. Clarke reaches a similar sense by his own route, glossing the petition as a request to be filled with goodness once emptied of evil. Wesley states the outcome plainly, that this qualifies and encourages them to give the sacrifices more pleasing to God than calves or oxen. Calvin uses the verse to attack a whole conception of repentance, since men bring forward mere trifles when they speak of it, imagining that fasts and muttered prayers and vowed pilgrimages will pacify God; the prophet, he says, sets out true repentance by its fruits instead.
3:
The three renunciations are counted and named. Ellicott lists them as the crying sins of the nation: expecting salvation from one great power, depending on another famed for war-horses and chariots, and giving divine names and homage to wrought images. Gill treats the verse as a continuation of the words the penitents are told to bring, a declaration that they will not do again what they did, looking to a foreign court for help and deliverance. Calvin makes the same sentence do double work: though the verbs are future, the speakers indirectly confess that they had already sinned grievously in these very ways, running here and there for safety, alienating themselves from God, and transferring to dumb images the honour due to him alone.

The clause about the fatherless is where the tenderness of the prayer is located. Ellicott glosses it as God's paternal love for the orphan, peculiarly applicable to a people now cast on a cold and fatherless world. Wesley widens the term to cover all who are destitute of strength in themselves and of help from others, and who, being sensible of that helplessness, look for it from the one who has power and mercy and wisdom to help; and he takes the mercy named to be both the fountain and the streams, free grace and rich bounty together.

The reply is read as an answer matched clause for clause to the petition. Gill notes that the promise to heal answers directly the request that iniquity be taken away, and works the metaphor out: sins are diseases, natural and hereditary, nauseous and mortal and incurable except by grace, backslidings are relapses and dangerous things, and there is one physician who heals both and never turns away anyone who applies to him. Henry states the principle behind the correspondence, that if we speak to God in good prayers he will speak to us in good promises, and that what is taken with us in coming to him may be taken home again for faith to feast on. Ellicott says only that if the foregoing is the offering of penitent lips, the reply is full of superlative grace.

Clarke numbers the parts of the answer as he had numbered the steps of the prayer. They had backslidden and been mortally wounded by the fall, and the author of life will heal the wounds; he will love them freely, which Clarke takes in a princely sense, a love that is beneficial and not merely affectionate, filling its objects with delight rather than only feeling it; and the anger is turned away because they have turned back. So, he concludes, God and man become friends.

Both Henry and Calvin dwell on the turning away of the anger, and for the same pastoral reason. Henry lays it down as the ground of every other favour promised, and adds the doctrine that God, justly and greatly angry as he is with sinners, is not implacable in his anger, which may be and shall be turned away from those who turn away from their iniquity. Calvin explains why the assurance had to be repeated at all: nothing is harder than to keep men depending on the one God and to quiet their minds, since when we embrace a promise of free pardon the flesh at once leads us to distrust, and we are harassed by the thought that we cannot dare to promise ourselves a propitious God while knowing how many reasons he has to be angry. It is because we are so inclined to harbour distrust, he says, that the prophet confirms the same truth again.
5:
The dew is read for what dew does in that climate. Clarke borrows a bishop's observations: in so hot a country dews are needed not only to refresh but to preserve life, and to feel the force of the promise one must add the beauty of the eastern lilies, the fragrance of the cedars, the spreading olives, the coolness of their shade and the aromatic smell they exhale. Gill takes the dew as coming down from heaven and applies the passage to a future conversion, following a rabbi in referring it to the latter day, when the promises will be made good in the blessings of grace. Wesley keeps it short: God will refresh and comfort those who return.

Calvin uses the promise to close an argument he has been making through the book. The people had been afflicted and ought to have read their own sins in it, but were so stupid as to imagine the adversities happened by chance; he had therefore taught at length that they would be miserable until they turned and unhappy in all their affairs until they obtained pardon. The change described here is the other half of that lesson, God showing himself so beneficent after the reconciliation that the fruit of it becomes visible.

The spreading branches are given both a natural and an ecclesiastical sense. Gill takes them for the propagation of the church and the interest of Christ in the world, in the first times of the gospel and again in the latter day, when churches shall be set up everywhere and the fulness of the Gentiles brought in. Wesley works the images separately: the new branches gather strength and multiply; the olive keeps green through winter and is rich in fruit, so the true Israel flourishes not in fruitless beauty but in lovely fruit even in winters of affliction; and the mountain named is famous not only for cedars but for the trees that yield frankincense and the flowers that perfume the air.

Whose shadow it is that shelters them divides the readers. Gill canvasses three answers, the shadow of the mountain or its trees, that of the church under which young converts sit with pleasure, or that of the Lord himself to whom Israel was called to return, and prefers the last. Calvin declines the question and settles the verb instead: the word rendered return properly means to be refreshed here, as in the psalm where the law is said to convert the soul, so the point is that once Israel begins to flourish again its shadow will be a vivifying one, restoring those who lie under it. Ellicott alters the syntax altogether, holding it more in accordance with the Hebrew idiom to render that the dwellers under its shadow shall once more cause the corn to grow.

The last images are handled for their exactness. Clarke explains why the comparison to corn is better than it looks: after the young plant has been a short time above ground the side leaves turn back to make way for the stalk and fall towards the earth with a withered appearance, so that a stranger seeing the field then could entertain no hope of a harvest. Wesley makes the same double point in miniature, the corn dying before it lives to bear fruit and the vine seeming dead in winter while sap and a fructifying virtue remain in it. Ellicott corrects the last word, which should be renown rather than scent, and notes that although the form of these promises is drawn from the external signs of national prosperity, corn and wine are throughout the scriptures the great symbols of spiritual refreshment. Clarke adds a curious rendering he found in the Targum, that they shall be gathered from the midst of their captivity, dwell under the shadow of his Christ, and the dead shall revive.
8:
Whether the renunciation is a promise or an argument is the first question. Henry reports both readings and prefers the second only to strengthen the first. On one rendering God is reasoning with the man, asking what he and idols have to do with each other, since there can be no concord between light and darkness, and so requiring the league with them to be broken before any covenant can be made; on the other, which Henry follows, God is promising to bring Ephraim to say it and to keep him to it. He then draws the theological point that matters most to him: God's promises to us are a far better security for the mortifying of sin than our promises to God, and whatever good we say or do at any time it is he who works it in us.

Calvin hears in the same words a confession rather than a resolution. The people are introduced speaking, as they were earlier in the chapter, deploring their blindness and folly and renouncing their superstitions for the future; and he takes that shame at oneself, joined to a detestation of the whole former life, as the testimony of true repentance. The discourse is concise, he grants, with a verb to be supplied, but its brevity contains nothing obscure.

Gill insists the speaker cannot be the Ephraim of the prophet's own day, who was so wedded and glued to his idols that there was no hope of getting him from them and who was therefore given up; it is Ephraim returning at God's call in the latter day. He then redefines the idols to fit that reading. Graven and molten images have not tempted the Jewish people since the captivity, so what is renounced must be the idols of the heart, the impiety and unbelief and rejection of the Messiah which at their conversion they will loathe and mourn over, together with the traditions of the elders which they now prefer even to the written word and will then relinquish for the gospel.

The evergreen tree raises a question about who is speaking. Clarke would attach the words to what precedes and make the whole a speech of God to Ephraim, following another translator, so that the sense is I have heard him and seen him as a flourishing tree, become strong and vigorous, from whose present healthiness a future increase may safely be anticipated. Ellicott takes the same view of the speaker, having God say that he is to Ephraim an evergreen tree of life and protection; he also prefers a slightly different reading indicated by the Greek, giving as for Ephraim, what has he to do with idols, and notes that the Hebrew for thy fruit plays on the name Ephraim, as it had earlier in the book. Wesley keeps the image on the human side, a weary traveller finding rest and safety under a thick tree, which is what protection under the Lord is like.

On the last clause all of them agree and press it. Clarke makes it the point of the verse: all goodness springs from a principle of grace planted in the soul, and as the earth cannot bear fruit without dew and rain and sun, neither can the soul of even the most pious bear fruit without a continual influence from above. Wesley reduces it to two words, of God alone. Henry has already made the same claim in his own idiom by referring the renunciation itself to God's working it in the heart, and Gill by referring the whole conversion to the influence of grace. Ellicott sets the promise and the fruit in the same sentence so that the source is unmistakable, and Clarke adds that God hears and observes the confession, so that the conversion is as complete as it is sincere.
9:
The closing question is read first for its function. Ellicott says the prophet hands his words over to all students of the ways of God, and notes that the exhortation is put as a question; in the later Hebrew writings wisdom and wise men take the place prophecy and prophets had held, wisdom being what interprets both the word and its fulfilment. Calvin gives a different account of the question, hearing amazement in it at how few yielded themselves to be taught. Clarke asks what things are meant and answers from the chapter: the backslidings and punishment of Israel, the mercy shown in their restoration, the work of sin in the heart and the work of grace in the soul.

Calvin uses the verse to explain why the book ends where it does. He is sure the prophet inculcated this often, having struggled with extreme obstinacy through the whole course of his preaching, so that seeing the people irreclaimable he went among them armed with confidence, telling men who thought themselves unpunished that they would find at last that the ways of the Lord are right. Prophets, he adds, reduced into brief heads at the end what they had taught at length, since it is absurd to suppose a man who held the office so long said only what could be gone through in three hours.

The pride the question rebukes is described in Calvin's century as much as the prophet's. Ungodly men think themselves especially acute when they laugh at piety and treat God's name with scorn, count it simplicity to embrace anything scripture contains, ask what faith is but foolish credulity, and taunt that to believe is to give up all judgment and be driven like mute cattle. There were many such, he supposes, in the prophet's day. The force of the question is therefore a challenge: if there is any grain of wisdom in you, you must acknowledge that I am sent and that what I declare is not men's invention. He closes by turning the word round: true wisdom is to obey God and embrace his word, the beginning of wisdom being the fear of him.

Clarke and Wesley fasten on the condition attached to understanding. Clarke says whoever endeavours to understand these things and lays his heart to them shall understand them. Wesley divides the ways in two, those God would have us walk in towards him and those in which he walks towards us in afflicting or comforting, and calls both righteous and equal. To walk in them is to approve them all, justifying the righteousness of the displeasure and confessing that mercy is remembered in the midst of judgment. Clarke states the same conclusion as an argument, that all God's conduct in justice and in mercy is right because he is too wise to err and too good to be unkind.

The last clause is the one they linger over, and they make it the more frightening for being about religious men. Wesley describes wilful sinners stumbling at the commands and still more at the judgments, casting off the one and hoping vainly to shift the other until they fall under the weight of their own sins. Clarke warns that men once good may fall in the way of righteousness itself, still using the ordinances and keeping company with God's people, if they do not depend on God for light and life and power. Henry sharpens it furthest. The same stone is a foundation to some and a stumbling-block to others, and what was ordained to life becomes death through their abuse of it, as the same sun softens wax and hardens clay; the most dangerous falls of all are those of men who fall in the ways of God, who split on the Rock of Ages and suck poison out of the balm.
